# Self-reported AI literacy and gendered self-efficacy: Evidence from Chinese adolescents

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

## Li Tian [a,](#telecommunications-policy) Wanyu Wu [a,\*](#telecommunications-policy) [,](https://orcid.org/0009-0002-0953-4079) Ya Tan [b,](#telecommunications-policy) Shilan Feng [c](#telecommunications-policy)

## ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT

### _Keywords:_ Artificial intelligence (AI) literacy has emerged as a key dimension of youth development, with 

AI literacy profound implications for education, labor markets, and social equity. Yet, disparities in AI lit- Digital divide eracy risk amplifying existing inequalities. This study examines gender differences in self- Gender gap

reported AI literacy among Chinese adolescents, conceptualizing self-reported AI literacy as a 

Self-efficacy AI reflection of self-efficacy. Drawing on Bandura's self-efficacy theory and a developmental- Chinese adolescents contextual perspective, we construct a multidimensional AI literacy index and employ counter-

factual analysis together with Blinder–Oaxaca decomposition to validate and decompose the gender gap. Using a stratified sample of adolescents from diverse backgrounds in China, the study reveals a gender gap in self-reported AI literacy, with males rating themselves higher than fe- males. This gap is heterogeneous across different dimensions of AI literacy and is most pro- nounced in the dimensions of Understanding, Ethics, and Society. The results further indicate that these differences are attributable both to perception biases and to actual disparities in observed background endowments. The findings highlight the risks of neglecting gendered self-efficacy gaps, which may perpetuate female exclusion from STEM opportunities, and underscore the importance of interventions that strengthen girls' AI self-efficacy. This research makes both theoretical and empirical contributions: it provides insights into the conceptualization and measurement of AI literacy, investigates the connection between AI literacy and self-efficacy, and 

offers policy-relevant implications for fostering more inclusive and equitable AI education.

## 1. Introduction

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping societies, economies, and labor markets worldwide. Alongside its transformative potential, AI also poses significant challenges for education systems, which must prepare the next generation to navigate, critically evaluate, and responsibly use AI technologies to support sustainable social development. As a result, the concept of AI literacy has emerged as a core competence for citizens in the digital era, encompassing not only technical knowledge of AI but also skills related to its ethical, social, and collaborative dimensions ([Lintner, 2024;](#data-availability) [Long & Magerko, 2020,](#data-availability) pp. 1–16). However, research consistently shows that confidence and proficiency in AI-related knowledge and skills are not evenly distributed across populations. More broadly, persistent gender gaps in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) have long been observed:

This phenomenon reflects broader patterns of biased self-efficacy in STEM, whereby females tend to undervalue their own abilities, reducing their likelihood of pursuing advanced study or careers in related fields ([Schunk & Pajares, 2002)](#data-availability). The pattern translates into structural inequality as AI becomes increasingly integrated into the technological world: there is a pronounced gender gap, with female representation notably lower in AI-related education and career pathways ([Interface-EU, 2024)](#data-availability). If left unaddressed, such disparities risk reinforcing existing inequalities in technology and further narrowing the global pipeline of AI talent.

While gendered inequalities in technology are global, the Chinese context presents distinctive challenges and opportunities. With more than 250 million adolescents, China is not only home to the world's largest youth population but also plays a central role in shaping the future global AI workforce. The country has introduced ambitious policies to integrate AI education into school curricula, recognizing AI literacy as a national priority ([Ministry of Education of the People’s Republic of China, 2024)](#data-availability). Yet, no systematic empirical evaluations have been conducted to assess the effectiveness of such initiatives. Given the scale of China's education system, if gender gaps in the AI domain are widespread, they may have profound implications for talent cultivation, equity in digital oppor- tunities, and the country's contribution to global AI development. Studying the Chinese case provides a critical lens for understanding how structural, educational, and cultural factors jointly shape gendered self-efficacy in emerging technological fields like AI—offering insights that extend beyond China to other societies undergoing rapid digital transformation.

When discussing AI, despite growing international attention to AI literacy, significant research gaps remain. For example, existing frameworks for AI literacy face two critical limitations. First, there is no consensus on how the construct and its measures should be defined. Second, on a global scale, the vast majority of AI literacy assessments rely on self-reports rather than performance-based or behavioral measures ([Lintner, 2024;](#data-availability) [Ng et al., 2021)](#data-availability), even though discrepancies are likely to exist between self-reported and behavioral outcomes ([Dang et al., 2020)](#data-availability). Within China, systematic empirical evidence on this topic is particularly rare. To avoid confusion between different modes of measurement, this study makes clear that our survey employed self-report scales and acknowledges that the results reflect self-reported AI literacy rather than actual AI competence. To gain a deeper understanding of the significance of self-reported AI literacy for adolescent AI users, we incorporate a distinct theoretical concept: self-efficacy. Self- efficacy, following Bandura, is a psychological construct referring to individuals' beliefs about their ability to accomplish tasks, and it is most commonly measured through self-report scales ([Bandura, 1997,](#data-availability) pp. 36–65). Self-reported AI literacy and AI self-efficacy both capture individuals' perceived competence in AI and are typically measured with self-report scales, which has led many studies to use them interchangeably ([Lintner, 2024)](#data-availability). However, they are not conceptually identical: self-reported AI literacy is a methodological approach to assessing perceived skills in AI, whereas self-efficacy is a broader psychological construct about one's belief in their ability to perform tasks. In this study, we therefore treat self-reported AI literacy as a reflection of AI self-efficacy, while making clear that it remains distinct from both actual AI literacy and the construct of self-efficacy. This framing enables us to investigate gender differences in perceived AI competence, which may diverge from actual ability yet strongly shape educational aspirations and career trajectories. Our study has two main objectives. 

RQ1: Do Chinese adolescents show gender-based differences in their self-reported AI literacy? RQ2: If so, which dimensions of self-reported AI literacy reflect such differences?

To address these questions, we analyze data from a large-scale survey of 1951 Chinese adolescents using a multi-method quan- titative approach. Findings reveal that female students report lower AI literacy overall and especially in Understanding, Application, Collaboration, Ethics, and Society dimensions. Results suggest that both self-perceptions and structural endowments contribute to the observed gender disparities, though their relative importance varies across dimensions.

This study makes four main contributions. First, whereas many existing studies rely on a single composite score or treat self-report indices as directly comparable across groups, we use Principal Component Analysis and Confirmatory Factor Analysis to construct and validate a multidimensional measure of self-reported AI literacy. Second, although prior studies occasionally acknowledge the con- ceptual ambiguity between self-reported literacy and actual competence, they rarely theorize this distinction explicitly. We therefore differentiate self-reported from actual AI competence and conceptualize self-reported AI literacy as an indicator of AI self-efficacy, drawing on Bandura's self-efficacy theory to clarify its psychological underpinnings. Third, while some research has documented gender disparities in AI-related domains, empirical evidence from China—especially theoretical explanations for why such gaps emerge—remains limited. Our study fills this gap by providing robust evidence on gender differences in Chinese adolescents' self- reported AI literacy and the mechanisms that may contribute to them. Finally, moving beyond descriptive mean comparisons that dominate prior work, we integrate counterfactual analysis with Blinder–Oaxaca decomposition to quantify the extent to which the observed gender gap can be attributed to differences in endowments (objective background characteristics) versus differences in coefficients (perception-related and unobserved factors). We further translate these analytical insights into targeted implications for educational practice and policy. Collectively, these contributions underscore the novelty and significance of this study within the evolving literature on AI literacy, self-efficacy, and gender inequality.

**The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.** Section 2 **reviews the literature on AI literacy, self-efficacy, and gender gaps in technology.** Section [3](#3-empirical-strategy-and-results) **outlines the empirical strategy and presents the results.** Section [4](#4-discussion) **discusses practical and policy implications and highlights the study's contributions.** Section [5](#5-limitation-and-future-research-directions) **acknowledges limitations and suggests directions for future research.**

## 2. Literature review

### _2.1._ _AI literacy: definitions and measurement_

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in everyday life, making AI literacy a critical competence for citizens. [Ng et al. (2021)](#data-availability) conceptualize AI literacy as the essential skills and knowledge required to live, learn, and work effectively in AI-driven soci- eties. Their framework highlights four core competencies: knowing and understanding AI concepts, using and applying AI tools, evaluating and creating AI systems, and addressing AI-related ethical issues. Building on this foundation, [Lintner (2024)](#data-availability) emphasizes that, despite the lack of a universally accepted definition, certain dimensions recur across most scales. These include technical un- derstanding, awareness of AI's societal impacts, and ethical considerations. However, divergences remain regarding whether higher-order competencies such as innovation or critical evaluation should be integrated within AI literacy. To bring greater coher- ence, some scholars draw on educational theory, notably Bloom's taxonomy of educational objectives ([Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001;](#data-availability) [Bloom et al., 1956)](#data-availability), to structure AI literacy into specific domains. Xu et al. (2025) extended this tradition by mapping Bloom's tax- onomy onto AI competency and further incorporating social and environmental dimensions, thereby proposing a lifelong competency framework for AI. Their model delineates eight dimensions: Identification, Understanding, Application, Evaluation, Collaboration, Innovation, Ethics, and Society. This study adopts Xu's framework as the basis for measuring AI literacy, given its comprehensiveness, strong theoretical grounding, developmental orientation, and relevance to the Chinese context.

In measuring AI literacy, most existing scales rely on self-reported measures; however, these instruments face concerns regarding questionable content validity ([Lintner, 2024)](#data-availability) as well as weak correlation with behavioral measures ([Dang et al., 2020)](#data-availability). Performance-based assessments, which could more reliably capture actual competencies, remain rare. These limitations underscore the need for more comprehensive and theoretically grounded instruments to evaluate AI literacy, as well as for clearer distinctions between self-reported and performance-based approaches.

### _2.2._ _Self-reported AI literacy as a reflection of AI self-efficacy_

Performance-based assessments of digital literacy—including AI literacy—typically involve task-based evaluations that measure actual skill levels. In contrast, self-reported instruments assess individuals' perceived abilities and are thus closely aligned with the psychological construct of self-efficacy. According to [Bandura (1997),](#data-availability) self-efficacy refers to an individual's belief in their capacity to execute the behaviors necessary to achieve specific goals. It is most commonly operationalized through self-report scales, where re- spondents rate their confidence in performing domain-specific tasks ([Pajares, 1996;](#data-availability) [Schwarzer & Jerusalem, 1995)](#data-availability). Numerous studies in educational psychology have demonstrated that higher self-efficacy is positively associated with motivation, persistence, and ac- ademic achievement ([Schunk & Pajares, 2002)](#data-availability). These dynamics are especially salient in emerging fields like AI, where students may lack concrete experience but still form beliefs about their abilities.

Although self-efficacy and self-reported AI literacy are conceptually distinct—one being a psychological construct and the other a domain-specific self-assessment—the boundary between them is often blurred in empirical research ([Lintner, 2024)](#data-availability). In practice, many studies use self-reported AI literacy scores interchangeably with AI self-efficacy, but this approach risks conflating conceptually distinct constructs and confusing measurement with theory. To clarify this ambiguity, the present study distinguishes between the theoretical constructs of AI literacy and self-efficacy, and the measurement approach of self-reported AI literacy. Here, self-reported AI literacy is treated as a reflection of AI self-efficacy—an indicator of adolescents' confidence in their AI capabilities rather than a measure of actual ability. This distinction is crucial for interpreting the results, as the observed gender gap reflects differences in perceived competence rather than objectively tested performance.

### _2.3._ _Gender, technology, and biased self-efficacy_

Research in science and technology education has long documented persistent gender gaps in digital competence and engagement, particularly during adolescence—a period marked by intensified identity formation and social comparison ([Encinas-Martín & Cherian, 2023)](#data-availability). While structural factors such as access and training partly contribute to these disparities, a growing body of evidence suggests that gender differences in self-perception and confidence play an equally critical role. Female students, even when performing on par with their male peers, often rate their abilities lower in STEM domains, a pattern attributed to internalized gender stereotypes and differential socialization ([Correll, 2001;](#data-availability) Wang & Degol, 2017).

This phenomenon aligns with the concept of biased self-efficacy—the discrepancy between actual competence and perceived ability. Such discrepancies arise because self-efficacy is shaped less by objective performance than by subjective experiences and social signals. Bandura's self-efficacy theory posits that individuals' beliefs in their capabilities are shaped by four primary sources: mastery experiences, vicarious experiences, verbal persuasion, and physiological and emotional states ([Artino, 2012;](#data-availability) [Bandura, 1997)](#data-availability). Mastery experiences, such as successfully completing AI-related tasks, provide the strongest reinforcement, while vicarious experiences (e.g. observing similar role models succeed), verbal persuasion (e.g. receiving credible encouragement), physiological and emotional states (e.g. managing confidence versus stress) also shape efficacy beliefs. These sources illustrate that self-efficacy is not formed in isolation but is socially embedded, shaped by cues, experiences, and cultural narratives that often reinforce male dominance in technical fields ([Schunk & Pajares, 2002)](#data-availability). In digital contexts, this manifests as confidence gaps that emerge early and widen over time, with girls exhibiting lower self-efficacy than boys in technology-related domains, including AI. As a result, girls are less likely to participate in optional technology courses, engage in AI-related activities, or envision themselves in tech careers—not necessarily due to lack of skill, 

but due to lower self-belief ([Master et al., 2021)](#data-availability). The effects of biased self-efficacy extend beyond the classroom. Studies show that lower self-perceived ability in technology can discourage girls from pursuing advanced training, reduce their persistence in STEM pathways, and ultimately shape long-term occupational outcomes (Zeldin & Pajares, 2000). In the context of AI, where the field is still emerging and educational standards are rapidly evolving, early confidence—or lack thereof—may play an outsized role in determining who participates in future inno- vation. Addressing gendered self-efficacy biases is therefore not only a question of individual development but also one of societal equity and inclusive technological progress.

## 3. Empirical strategy and results

### _3.1._ _Questionnaire distribution and_ _data collection_

This study collaborated with an independent third-party survey company ePanel[1](#3-empirical-strategy-and-results) [to conduct an online questionnaire targeting ](#3-empirical-strategy-and-results)adolescents from various city tiers and socioeconomic backgrounds across China. The questionnaire consists of 12 choice items concerning personal background and 32 self-assessment items measuring AI literacy. The latter were measured using a five-point Likert scale (1 = Strongly Disagree to 5 = Strongly Agree). Prior to the main data collection, a pilot survey of 200 adolescents was conducted to refine item wording and sequencing for clarity and age-appropriate comprehension. For the main study, 2200 questionnaires were distributed using a stratified random sampling design to ensure representativeness across regions, school types, and demographics. China was first divided into three broad geographic–economic regions (eastern, central, and western), which were further stratified by urban, county, and rural areas. Within each stratum, schools were randomly selected at the primary, junior secondary, and senior secondary levels, followed by random sampling of classes and students. To improve inclusivity, the sample also included schools from minority regions and special education institutions. The questionnaire is provided in the Appendix.

Data collection took place between April and June 2024. Following data collection, ePanel conducted an initial round of cleaning using its standardized quality-control procedures, which included IP–region consistency checks, device uniqueness verification, and the removal of responses completed in less than 10 min, among others. After this stage, 2043 valid responses were delivered to the authors. We then conducted a second round of cleaning and excluded 13 cases with missing answers, as well as 79 cases that failed a consistency check (Q14 vs. Q36: “I can clearly understand my needs and expectations when using AI”). All respondents passed the embedded attention-check item (Q45: “Please select ‘Strongly Agree’ for this question”). The final analytic sample comprised 1951 adolescents aged 12 to 18, with a gender distribution of 50.4 % female and 49.6 % male. The valid sample covers a wide range of demographic characteristics, including first-tier cities (20.7 %), second-tier cities (30.7 %), and other cities (30.4 %); townships (9.5 %), rural areas (8.7 %), ensuring regional diversity. Further details of the sample characteristics can be found in [Appendix Table A1.](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement) The selection of the 12–18 age group is grounded in careful considerations. According to the World Health Organization (WHO, 2014), adolescents are defined as individuals aged 10–19. In this study, we focus on adolescents aged 12–18. Prior literature suggests adolescents aged 12 to 18 are significant users of AI technologies, frequently interacting with smart devices, educational applications, and social media, making this group especially relevant for exploring AI usage intentions ([Mustafaoglu et al., 2018˘](#data-availability) [)](#data-availability). In China, students aged 12 to 15 typically attend junior high school, while those aged 15 to 18 are in senior high school. Therefore, the 12–18 age range effectively captures the span of secondary education in China, a critical period during which students' cognitive, social, and digital competencies—including AI literacy—undergo significant development.

Throughout the data collection phase, all procedures strictly followed ethical standards to ensure the confidentiality and security of participant information. Informed consent was obtained from all respondents, with proxy consent granted by parents or legal guardians in the case of minors. To protect individual identities, all data were anonymized prior to analysis and stored securely, with access restricted solely to research-related use.

### _3.2._ _Construction of the self-reported AI literacy index_

Based on a comprehensive review of prior literature on the conceptualization and measurement of AI literacy, and in particular drawing on Xu's (2025) _Lifelong Competency Framework for Generation AI_, this study conceptualizes AI literacy into a structured framework. Building on Bloom's taxonomy of educational objectives, Xu mapped the cognitive stages emphasized by Bloom, including knowledge, comprehension, application, and evaluation—onto the context of the intelligent society, and enriched the taxonomy by incorporating collaboration and innovation dimensions on the social-interactional side, as well as ethics and society dimensions on the socio-environmental side, thereby addressing Bloom's limited attention to contextual and societal factors. The result is a four-domain AI competency model—Identification and Understanding, Application and Evaluation, Collaboration and Innovation, and Ethics and Society—which is further disaggregated into eight core dimensions: identification, understanding, application, evaluation, 

1 ePanel, established in 2006, is a certified professional data provider licensed by the National Bureau of Statistics of China to conduct foreign- related surveys. The company is a member of the European Society for Opinion and Marketing Research (ESOMAR) and holds a vice-presidency in the China Marketing Research Association (CMRA), adhering to quality-control standards issued jointly by the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) and ESOMAR, as well as by the Global Research Business Network (GRBN) and ESOMAR. It maintains long-term collaborations with leading universities and research institutes in China through formal procurement procedures and has no financial or organizational conflict of interest with this study or its authors.

collaboration, innovation, ethics, and society. Identification refers to the ability to recognize AI-related concepts, activities, risks, and needs. Understanding captures users' comprehension of the logic of AI operations in social and technical contexts. Application assesses how well individuals manage digital identity, use AI tools, create content with AI, and engage in AI-supported social interactions. Evaluation measures the ability to critically assess AI-related information, content, and products. Collaboration emphasizes skills in human–AI and team interaction, resource coordination, and open sharing. Innovation reflects the capability to optimize AI for technical, content, knowledge, and problem-solving innovations. Ethics concerns the responsible use of AI under the principles of information security, privacy protection, human-centered values, and inclusiveness. Finally, Society highlights awareness, engage- ment, and responsibility in addressing public issues and contributing to social well-being through AI.

Following Xu's interpretation of the eight dimensions, this study measures self-reported AI literacy across these dimensions, with each dimension assessed through four sub-competencies, yielding a total of 32 survey items. The mapping of the 32 items onto the eight dimensions is shown in [Fig. 1,](#33-confirmatory-factor-analysis-of-the-ai-literacy-scale) with the full survey instrument provided in [Appendix D](#appendix-d-full-survey-instrument) and descriptive statistics in [Appendix Table A2.](#appendix-d-full-survey-instrument) Since the figure only displays abbreviated labels for the 32 sub-competencies, [Appendix Table B2](#appendix-d-full-survey-instrument) includes a detailed mapping table that links each survey item to its corresponding sub-competency and dimension.

To further quantify self-reported AI literacy, the Self-reported AI Literacy Index is constructed using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) based on responses to the 32 survey questions.

PCA is a dimensionality reduction technique that extracts the most informative components from a dataset while minimizing in- formation loss. Following established practice in constructing literacy and technology indices ([Soundararajan et al., 2023;](#data-availability) Yadav, Chhabra, Singh, & Hazarika, 2024; Zhou et al., 2025), we apply PCA to generate an index that captures the core variations in self-reported AI literacy across respondents, ensuring that the measure is data-driven, statistically robust, and comparable to related studies. To assess the adequacy of this approach, we report standard diagnostics: the overall KMO statistic was 0.981, the determinant of the correlation matrix was near zero, and Bartlett's test of sphericity (χ[^2](496) = 28,131.31, p _\<_ .001) rejected the null of no intercorrelation among variables. These results also indicate that the data are suitable for Factor Analysis. Besides, we also conduct measurement invariance tests across gender, ensuring that gender differences in AI literacy are not driven by measurement bias. The SEM model demonstrated good fit, as indicated by a non-significant model-versus-saturated test (χ[^2]= 0.000, df = 0) and a highly significant baseline-versus-saturated test (χ[^2]= 202.27, p _\<_ .001).

Additionally, as a robustness check, we verify that an alternative Factor Analysis approach yields highly correlated results (see [Appendix Table B2)](#appendix-d-full-survey-instrument), confirming the index's methodological soundness. Beyond the overall self-reported AI literacy index, we further examine self-reported AI literacy through the eight dimensions (Identification, Understanding, Application, Evaluation, Collaboration, Innovation, Ethics, Society) in order to identify the specific aspects where gender differences are most pronounced. This dimensional analysis allows us to pinpoint the sources of variation rather than attributing differences solely to the overall index. To provide an overview of the data set, [Appendix Table A1](#appendix-d-full-survey-instrument) reports descriptive statistics for some of the key variables, including the self-reported AI literacy index, its sub-dimensions, and the covariates. This summary allows us to assess the distributional properties of self-reported AI literacy across different groups and serves as the foundation for subsequent empirical analyses. To facilitate com- parison by gender, [Appendix Table A3](#appendix-d-full-survey-instrument) presents the descriptive statistics separately for male and female respondents.

### _3.3._ _Confirmatory Factor Analysis of the AI literacy scale_

To further validate the eight-dimensional AI literacy scale, we conducted a Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) using the complete

dataset of 2043 valid responses collected before applying exclusion criteria for the final analytic sample. CFA rigorously tests whether the observed data fit the hypothesized factor structure, providing psychometric evidence for construct validity. The model was esti- mated using Maximum Likelihood (ML) estimation, which is appropriate for five-point Likert scales with large sample sizes. Model fit was evaluated using multiple indices following established criteria: χ[^2]/df _\<_ 3.0, Comparative Fit Index (CFI) and Tucker- Lewis Index (TLI) _\>_ 0.90, Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA) _\<_ 0.08, and Goodness of Fit Index (GFI) _\>_ 0.90. Reliability was assessed via Cronbach's alpha (α) and Composite Reliability (CR), with thresholds of 0.70. Convergent validity was evaluated through Average Variance Extracted (AVE _\>_0.50), and discriminant validity was tested using the Fornell-Larcker criterion. Model Fit. The CFA demonstrated good fit: χ[^2](436) = 2220.27, p _\<_ .001; CFI = 0.936; TLI = 0.927; RMSEA = 0.045 \[90 % CI: 0.043, 0.047\]; GFI = 0.922. Although the χ[^2]/df ratio (5.09) exceeded the ideal threshold, this is attributable to the large sample size, as the chi-square statistic is highly sensitive to sample size. All alternative fit indices met or exceeded recommended standards, con- firming good model fit. Detailed fit statistics are provided in [Appendix Table C1.](#appendix-d-full-survey-instrument)

All 32 items demonstrated significant standardized factor loadings ranging from 0.754 to 1.695 (p _\<_ .001), with 100 % of items exceeding the recommended threshold of 0.70. z-values ranged from 20.43 to 31.70, providing strong evidence of convergent validity. Reliability and Validity. Cronbach's alpha ranged from 0.689 to 0.814 (M = 0.738), with seven of eight dimensions meeting the 

0.70 threshold. Composite Reliability ranged from 0.948 to 1.169, substantially exceeding the 0.70 criterion for all dimensions. AVE values ranged from 0.820 to 2.262, all surpassing the 0.50 threshold and confirming convergent validity. Note that AVE values exceeding 1.0 result from using unstandardized factor loadings, which is statistically permissible in structural equation modeling. Discriminant validity was established using the Fornell-Larcker criterion: the square root of AVE for each dimension exceeded its correlations with all other dimensions. Inter-dimension correlations ranged from 0.162 (Innovation–Understanding) to 0.355 (Eval- uation–Application), indicating that dimensions are conceptually distinct yet related. Reliability and validity indices are summarized in [Appendix Table C3](#appendix-d-full-survey-instrument) and C4.

In sum, the CFA provides robust psychometric evidence supporting the eight-dimensional AI literacy framework. The model demonstrates excellent fit, and all items exhibit strong and significant factor loadings. The comprehensive reliability and validity assessments confirm that the scale is internally consistent, convergently valid, and discriminantly valid.

### _3.4._ _Empirical strategy_

To address the two research questions, we employ two complementary research approaches based on survey data: counterfactual analysis and Blinder–Oaxaca decomposition. Counterfactual analysis aims to determine whether gender differences exist in self- reported AI literacy, while Blinder–Oaxaca decomposition is used to validate the differences, as well as to explore which di- mensions of self-reported AI literacy reflect such differences.

Counterfactual analysis has been widely applied in fields such as economics, education, policy evaluation, and sociology, partic- ularly in research contexts involving causal inference. Its core lies in constructing a counterfactual scenario to estimate what an in- dividual's outcome would have been under an alternative condition (e.g., gender, treatment status, etc.) ([Morgan & Winship, 2015)](#data-availability). In this study, counterfactual analysis involves constructing predictive models to calculate self-reported AI literacy scores for male and female respondents separately, and estimating counterfactual AI literacy scores by applying each gender-specific model to the opposite group. This approach is designed to uncover systematic gender differences in self-reported AI literacy by holding structural factors constant—much more rigorous than group mean comparisons, which will conflate perception gaps with background disparities ([Morgan & Winship, 2015)](#data-availability). Counterfactual analysis is particularly well suited for analyzing subjective self-assessments, as it reveals whether gendered gaps persist even when objective circumstances are equal—thus capturing deeper cognitive asymmetries. The model's predictors are grounded in Bandura's self-efficacy theory and further contextualized through the lens of developmental contextualism, with specific attention to the structural features of Chinese socio-cultural settings. Given that Bandura's four primary sources of self-efficacy—mastery experiences, vicarious experiences, verbal persuasion, and physiological and emotional states ([Artino, 2012)](#data-availability)—are inherently subjective and socially embedded, their operationalization requires the use of observable variables that capture manifestations of these sources, in order to reduce risks of endogeneity and common method bias. Building on this foundation, the model incorporates developmental contextualism, which conceptualizes individual development as a dynamic interaction between biological, psychological, and multiple environmental systems—such as family, school, and broader social structures ([Mayes & Lewis, 2012)](#data-availability). These theoretical perspectives inform the construction of the model structured along three interrelated dimen- sions—individual, parental, and socioeconomic—conceptualized as a nested system of developmental contexts rather than as inde- pendent sets of predictors. The model is specified as follows: 

AIi = α+βIndividuali+γParentali+ηSocioeconomici + FEi+εi 

Where _AIi_ is the self-reported AI literacy index. _FEi_ denotes fixed effects for grade level, residence type, and school type. _εi_ is the error term capturing remaining unobserved factors. _Individual, Parental,_ and _Socioeconomic_ represent the three conceptual sets of predictors. The individual dimension captures students' educational characteristics, with self-reported academic performance as the key indicator. The parental dimension includes the highest educational attainment of each parent and whether either parent works in an AI-related field. The socioeconomic dimension captures household-level indicators such as car ownership and travel frequency. To elaborate, self-reported academic performance may influence adolescents through perceived academic value and self- confidence, shaping both emotional and motivational processes. Parents’ educational backgrounds and involvement in AI-related fields contribute to the intergenerational transmission of cultural capital ([Bourdieu, 1986)](#data-availability), providing vicarious experiences and verbal persuasion. Meanwhile, material resources and social capital embedded in households create structural conditions that facilitate mastery and vicarious learning opportunities in AI-related activities; students in more advantaged socioeconomic environments may also benefit from more supportive emotional and cognitive contexts.

In addition, prior research has documented systematic contextual differences across grade levels, residential tiers, and school sectors—such as developmental variation ([Bandura, 1997)](#data-availability), disparities in technology access and digital literacy (van Dijk, 2006), and differences in educational resources ([Hanushek & Woessmann, 2011)](#data-availability). Accordingly, grade level, residence type (e.g., first-tier cities, second-tier cities, villages), and school type (public, private, or other) are included as fixed effects (FE). These variables represent key contextual factors that shape students’ learning environments, and because they vary by discrete groups rather than along a continuous scale, they are more appropriately represented through dummy variables rather than treated as continuous regressors. Incorporating them as fixed effects absorbs these structural differences without imposing functional-form assumptions.

After estimating separate models for males and females, we proceed as follows: (1) Applying female respondents' data to the male model to generate counterfactual predictions of their self-reported AI literacy level—i.e., how women would perceive their AI literacy if they evaluated themselves based on the male model. We then compare this predicted value with their actual self-reported AI literacy; 

2. Applying male respondents' data to the female model to generate counterfactual predictions of their self-reported AI literacy level—i.e., how men would perceive their AI literacy if they evaluated themselves based on the female model. Again, this estimated value is compared to their actual self-reported AI literacy level. The differences between the counterfactual and actual self-reported AI literacy levels for each gender provide a measure of the gender gap in self-reported AI literacy.

The second method applies the Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition to further quantify and specify the gender gap in self-reported AI literacy. The Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition is widely used in labor economics and gender studies to decompose differences in out- comes (e.g., wages, educational attainment) into explained and unexplained components ([Lesik & Fallahi, 2011)](#data-availability). In our case, this method allows us to: (1) decompose the gender gap in self-reported AI literacy into components attributable to observable factors (e.g., individual, parental, and socioeconomic characteristics); (2) identify the unexplained component, which captures gender differences that persist even after controlling for observable characteristics—often interpreted as arising from differences in self-perception, biases, or unmeasured factors. It is important to note that this method relies on key assumptions, including linearity of the rela- tionship between predictors and the outcome and correct model specification, which may be restrictive in our context. We therefore use the decomposition as an illustrative tool to highlight the relative contributions of observable versus unexplained factors, and we caution against interpreting the unexplained component as definitive causal evidence. The Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition is employed to provide a robust quantitative assessment of the gender gap in self-reported AI literacy and to examine its contribution to broader patterns of gender disparity.

### _3.5._ _Empirical results_

#### _3.5.1._ _Counterfactual analysis_

We construct gender-specific OLS prediction models in which the dependent variable is self-reported AI literacy. Specifically, we estimate separate regressions for the female and male samples of self-reported AI literacy on the explanatory variables, and use the resulting coefficients for subsequent prediction. The regression estimates for these models are reported in [Appendix Table E1.](#appendix-d-full-survey-instrument) Results show that Academic Performance emerges as the strongest and most consistent predictor of self-reported AI literacy for both genders, significant at the 1 % level, suggesting that higher academic achievement is closely associated with higher AI literacy regardless of gender. Household economic conditions also matter: family travel frequency (_Family Travel_) shows a positive and significant associ- ation, particularly for males, indicating that broader exposure to diverse environments may enhance AI awareness. In contrast, parental AI engagement (_Parental AI_) does not exhibit a significant effect in either group. Regarding parental education, mother's education is positively associated with AI literacy among females (significant at the 10 % level), while father's education shows no effect. This pattern suggests that maternal educational background may play a more prominent role in shaping daughters' AI self- efficacy, pointing to a potential family-level pathway for addressing technological gender gaps. This result is consistent with a growing body of evidence highlighting the distinct influence of maternal education on children's cognitive and skill outcomes ([Cermakova et al., 2023;](#data-availability) [Guo et al., 2024;](#data-availability) [Harding, 2015a;](#data-availability) [Harding et al., 2015b)](#data-availability).

The R-squared values indicate that the model explains 16.8 % of the variance in self-reported AI literacy for females and 11.8 % for males, suggesting that the included predictors account for a larger proportion of self-reported AI literacy variance among females. Following the empirical strategy, all models include fixed effects (FE) for residence type, grade level, and school type to absorb

contextual heterogeneity across learning environments. Next, we evaluate the explanatory power of the prediction models. Specifically, we use the female model to predict self-reported AI literacy for the female sample and compare the predicted values with observed self-reported AI literacy levels. Similarly, we perform the same assessment using the male model for the male sample. The results indicate a close alignment between the predicted and observed mean values for both groups, with consistent mean values but some discrepancies in standard deviations. As shown in [Table 1,](#35-empirical-results) the mean predicted self-reported AI literacy aligns exactly with the observed mean for both females (− 0.057) and males (0.297), which reflects a model fit to some extent, as well as the mechanical property of OLS. However, the predicted standard de- viations (1.276 for females, 1.073 for males) are notably smaller than the observed standard deviations (3.697 for females, 3.333 for males), suggesting that while the models accurately estimate average AI literacy, they may not fully capture the variability present in the data. Overall, while the models are informative in capturing central tendencies, their explanatory power may be interpreted with caution.

Building on the established prediction models, we now estimate the gender gap in self-reported AI literacy by generating coun- terfactual self-reported AI literacy levels. This allows us to assess how individuals would evaluate their self-reported AI literacy if they adopted the perception framework of the opposite gender.

First, we compare the observed self-reported AI literacy levels of female respondents with their counterfactual self-reported AI literacy levels, which are predicted using the male model. As shown in [Table 1,](#35-empirical-results) the mean observed self-reported AI literacy for females is − 0.057, whereas their counterfactual mean, if evaluated using the male model, increases to 0.232. The difference of 0.335 suggests

that if females perceived their AI literacy using the male assessment framework, their self-reported AI literacy scores would be higher, indicating a potential underestimation of self-reported AI literacy among females.

Second, we conduct the same counterfactual estimation for male respondents by applying the female model to predict their self- reported AI literacy levels. The results show that the mean observed self-reported AI literacy for males is 0.297, while their coun- terfactual self-reported AI literacy, if evaluated using the female model, decreases to 0.111. The difference of 0.186 implies that if males assessed their AI literacy through the female perception framework, they would report lower self-reported AI literacy levels, suggesting a tendency for males to report higher levels of their AI competency compared to females.

Fig. 2 shows the observed and counterfactual distributions of self-reported AI literacy for females and males, respectively. The comparison also reveals clear gender gaps: females tend to report lower levels of their AI capabilities, while males tend to report higher levels of theirs. These findings provide empirical evidence of a gender gap in self-reported AI literacy, and highlight the importance of considering perceptual biases when evaluating gender disparities in AI literacy.

#### _3.5.2._ _Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition results_

To further validate the existence of the gender gap in self-reported AI literacy, we apply the Blinder–Oaxaca decomposition to partition the overall gender disparity in self-reported AI literacy into explained and unexplained components. Table 2 presents the decomposition results, with Column (1) reporting the results for overall self-reported AI literacy, and Columns (2) to (9) providing results for the eight dimensions of self-reported AI literacy. In interpreting these results, the endowment component reflects gender differences in observed characteristics, such as academic performance, parental education, or socioeconomic background. This part reflects how unequal distributions of these factors contribute to the AI literacy gap. The coefficient component, by contrast, is espe- cially informative because it reflects differences in how those characteristics translate into AI literacy, represents the unexplained portion of the gap (e.g. perception biases), and thereby directly captures gendered differences in AI self-efficacy. In other words, even when males and females have similar endowments, their self-rating could differ, pointing to perception biases, unobserved factors, or systematic differences.

The first column of Table 2 shows that males report a self-reported AI literacy score 0.344 higher than females, a statistically significant gap at the 5 % level. Decomposing this difference, we find that endowment differences explain 0.247 of the gap, suggesting that observable factors such as academic performance, parental education, and socioeconomic background contribute to gender disparities in self-reported AI literacy. The coefficients component (0.275) is slightly larger than the endowments component (0.247), suggesting that perception-related differences contribute meaningfully to the observed gap. However, the negative interaction term (− 0.178) indicates that the mapping from endowments to self-reported AI literacy differs by gender and offsets part of the explained and coefficient effects.

Taking a closer look at the sub-dimensions, the gender gap persists across all eight, though the magnitude and underlying mechanisms differ.

For Identification (Column 2), the male–female difference (0.025) is not statistically significant, suggesting broadly similar levels of AI awareness across genders. Both the endowment and coefficient components are small, indicating limited systematic disparities in this dimension.

For Understanding (Column 3), the gender gap is 0.069 and significant at the 5 % level. Endowments explain 0.035 of this dif- ference, while the coefficients component (0.057) accounts for a somewhat larger share, suggesting that perception or self-evaluation differences contribute meaningfully to this disparity (in males rating their Understanding higher than females). For Application (Column 4), the gender gap (0.050) reaches significance at the 10 % level only. Most of this difference is associated with endowment effects (0.039), implying that observable background characteristics modestly shape the male–female difference in self-reported application skills. The coefficients component is positive but not statistically significant, indicating limited evidence of perception-related differences in this dimension.

For Evaluation (Column 5), the gender difference (0.040) is not statistically significant. For Collaboration (Column 6), the gender gap of 0.058 is significant at the 5 % level. The endowment component (0.043) suggests that background factors account for much of the observed difference, while the coefficients component (0.048) is not statistically significant.

For Innovation (Column 7), the gender gap (0.032) is not statistically significant. For Ethics (Column 8), the gender gap is 0.073 and significant at the 1 % level, marking one of the more pronounced disparities. The coefficients component (0.053) exceeds the endowment effect, suggesting that perception or self-evaluation differences play an important role in how males and females assess their understanding of AI ethics.

Finally, in the Society dimension (Column 9), the gender gap (0.062) is significant at the 5 % level. Here again, the coefficients component (0.056) is notably larger than the endowment effect (0.043), indicating that perception-related factors are an important correlate of the male–female difference in this domain.

Overall, the Blinder–Oaxaca decomposition results show that gender differences in self-reported AI literacy are present but het- erogeneous across dimensions. Some disparities—particularly in Understanding, Ethics, and Society—are statistically robust and appear to be more strongly associated with perception-related mechanisms, reflecting underlying differences in AI self-efficacy, whereas others (e.g., Application, Collaboration) are smaller in magnitude and primarily related to observable endowments. Di- mensions such as Identification, Evaluation, and Innovation exhibit limited or statistically weak gender differences. These findings suggest that while males tend to report higher levels of AI literacy than females, the size of the gender differences and the mechanisms underlying them vary across dimensions.

## 4. Discussion

AI technologies are profoundly reshaping education, communication, and economic life, making AI literacy a core civic compe- tency and a potential determinant of future social stratification. Individuals with higher AI literacy can critically evaluate AI-generated content, use AI tools productively, and protect their privacy and rights while mitigating risks. At the societal level, fostering balanced and healthy AI literacy development contributes to economic productivity, reduces digital inequalities, and fosters more inclusive governance systems. This broad importance of AI literacy also points to its unequal distribution. The digital divide has been widely studied as a persistent inequality in digital literacy across populations, with well-documented negative consequences. Although research on AI literacy gaps remains nascent, scholars point out that the AI literacy divide parallels the digital divide, encompassing disparities in access, skills, and outcomes ([Carter, Liu, & Cantrell, 2020)](#data-availability). If viewed as a new manifestation of the digital divide, the AI literacy divide is almost inevitable—yet, given AI's status as an emerging technology, its causes, forms, and consequences are more fluid and evolving. Within this evolving landscape, we noticed that differences in AI self-efficacy may further intensify the divide. Self-efficacy shapes the extent of individuals choosing to engage with AI and persist in learning, thereby causing and magnifying disparities. Adolescence (ages 12–18) is a particularly critical period for developing such self-beliefs, as it is when cognitive, emotional, and technological competencies expand rapidly ([Livingstone & Helsper, 2007)](#data-availability). Fostering AI self-efficacy during this stage is partic- ularly essential to ensure equitable participation in the AI era.

**Against this background, this study conceptualizes self-reported AI literacy as a reflection of AI self-efficacy, to empiri-** **cally examine how adolescents' AI self-efficacy translates into reported literacy levels and contributes to gendered dispar-** **ities. Our findings reveal a gender-based difference of self-reported AI literacy (**RQ1)**, with males consistently reporting higher competence in Understanding, Application, Collaboration, Ethics, and Society dimensions (**RQ2**). Importantly, the sources of these disparities vary: Application and Collaboration gaps are linked primarily to structural resource differences, while Understanding, Ethics, and Society gaps stem mainly from perception-based self-assessments. One possible explana-** **tion is that Application and Collaboration rely on concrete opportunities and resources, to which boys often have greater access, whereas dimensions involving critical judgment and ethical reflection (Understanding, Ethics, and Society) are more vulnerable to girls' systematic underestimation of their tech abilities. By unpacking these mechanisms, the Blinder–Oaxaca decomposition not only identifies which dimensions display gender disparities (**RQ2**) but also clarifies how both structural and perceptual factors jointly sustain the self-reported AI literacy divide.**

The findings of this study reveal a concerning trend: regardless of their actual competencies, girls tend to report relatively low AI self-efficacy, suggesting that they do not believe they are capable enough of mastering AI like boys do. This lack of confidence may deter them from engaging in AI-related learning and limit their pursuit of future opportunities in related careers. Consistent with Bandura's framework of the four sources of self-efficacy, these patterns may reflect girls' relative lack of task-based practice oppor- tunities in AI (mastery experiences), the scarcity of female role models in the field (vicarious experiences), and subtle classroom or broader societal cues that reinforce gender stereotypes and reduce affirming feedback (verbal persuasion). Meanwhile, boys may benefit from more frequent affirming feedback and male-dominated exemplars in technology fields. Addressing these dynamics re- quires deliberate efforts to strengthen adolescent girls' AI self-efficacy. Such initiatives can help expand the talent pipeline for AI innovation, increase women's access to professional opportunities, and challenge entrenched gender norms—particularly in East Asian societies, where expectations around female domesticity remain pervasive. Advancing gender equity in AI also supports the devel- opment of a more inclusive and just technological ecosystem, aligning with global agendas such as Sustainable Development Goal 5: Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls (United Nations, 2015), as well as UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2021).

Building such an inclusive ecosystem requires not only individual-level interventions but also systemic policy and curriculum reforms. Worldwide, governments are beginning to incorporate AI into school systems, emphasizing technical competence alongside ethics and social responsibility (UNESCO, 2021). In China, these efforts are unfolding at both national and local levels. At the national level, the Ministry of Education issued guidance on how to teach AI in primary and middle schools ([Ministry of Education of the People’s Republic of China, 2024)](#data-availability), outlining a phased curriculum framework from experiential learning in early grades to project-based exploration in secondary schools, supported by teacher training and school–industry partnerships. Regionally, provinces have launched pilot initiatives tailored to local contexts: for example, Jiangsu plans to establish 60 AI experimental schools by 2027 ([Jiangsu Provincial Department of Education, 2025)](#data-availability); Shandong is introducing AI literacy courses across all grades and building innovation research bases ([Shandong Provincial Department of Education, 2025)](#data-availability). At the city level, Beijing has announced that, starting in the 2025 fall semester, AI courses will be incorporated into Nine-Year Compulsory Education (six years of primary school and three years of junior secondary school) with at least eight class hours per year, either as stand-alone or integrated modules ([2025)](#data-availability); similarly, Hangzhou has made AI courses compulsory across all primary and secondary schools and is simultaneously enhancing teacher training in intelligent tools and data security (Nurmamat, 2025). Despite the breadth of these initiatives, they pay little explicit attention to gender-specific disparities, leaving a gap where bias-aware pedagogy, female mentorship, and inclusive curriculum design could be systematically embedded. While these initiatives signal promising momentum, they remain in the early stages of development. Their long-term impact will hinge not only on faithful implementation but also on systematic monitoring and evaluation of outcomes. It is essential to assess whether these policies are being effectively enacted across contexts and to refine them dynamically in response to observed challenges.

Building upon these ongoing initiatives, we put forward some policy recommendations for the five dimensions that show strong gender gaps, with a specific focus on strengthening adolescent girls' AI self-efficacy:

To address the gender gap in Understanding, policies should expand opportunities for girls to engage with data, algorithms, and AI 

concepts at earlier stages. National and provincial AI curricula could include gender-sensitive modules and task-based projects that build mastery experiences. Establishing female role-model databases and inviting women professionals into classrooms would provide vicarious experiences that strengthen girls' confidence in understanding technical foundations. For Application, the gap is primarily driven by structural differences in access to resources. Interventions should focus on expanding girls' access to AI learning tools, hands- on practice opportunities, and skill development in digital identity management, AI tool use, and creative production. Schools could establish “Girls in AI” clubs, competitions, and participation awards that encourage active use of AI tools in safe environments. Partnerships with technology companies can further provide equitable access to AI applications, while also embedding digital safety and privacy protection training. The Collaboration dimension calls for measures to promote gender-balanced teamwork in AI-related projects. Policies should incentivize schools and extracurricular programs to create mixed-gender teams, ensuring that girls participate equally in leadership and technical roles. Mentorship schemes connecting female students with women scientists and industry pro- fessionals can help counter implicit biases in team settings. Community networks and peer-support platforms should also be strengthened to reduce isolation and build collective efficacy. In the Ethics dimension, where perception gaps are particularly pro- nounced, interventions must cultivate girls' critical engagement with ethical issues. Curricula should integrate gender-inclusive case studies on privacy, security, and algorithmic bias, while public discourse should highlight women's voices in debates on AI governance. Institutional safeguards—such as data protection norms in schools—can reinforce these lessons and normalize gender-sensitive ap- proaches to responsible AI use. Media representation also plays a key role: shifting portrayals of women in science and technology from appearance-focused to achievement-oriented narratives can foster confidence in engaging with ethical discussions. For Society, where girls systematically underrate their ability to use AI in civic participation, initiatives should encourage female students to engage with public issues through AI-supported platforms. Programs that integrate digital volunteering, public-interest projects, or AI-for-good challenges into school curricula can showcase how AI contributes to social responsibility. Increasing women's visibility in social campaigns and appointing female spokespersons in technology-related public communication can further strengthen girls' belief in their capacity to contribute meaningfully to society through AI.

Additionally, the study yields supplementary insights into the drivers of adolescents' self-reported AI literacy. Self-reported aca- demic performance emerges as the most consistent predictor across genders, underscoring the strong association between general scholastic achievement and confidence in AI-related competencies. Moreover, parental education shows a gendered pattern: mothers' educational attainment is positively associated with daughters' self-reported AI literacy. This points to a potential mother-to-daughter transmission channel, consistent with Bandura's self-efficacy theory, in which mothers may foster girls' efficacy beliefs through role modeling, verbal persuasion, and emotional support. By contrast, we detect no corresponding paternal effect. This absence may reflect entrenched role segmentation in educational involvement, where fathers remain less engaged in everyday learning processes, or a broader undervaluing of paternal contributions to the cultivation of girls' self-beliefs in technical fields. Such findings highlight the importance of interrogating gendered parenting practices and addressing the systematic underrepresentation of fathers in fostering daughters' technological self-efficacy.

This study offers several contributions across theoretical, methodological, and practical domains. Empirically, it is among the first to investigate gender gaps in self-reported AI literacy among Chinese adolescents. Conceptually, it connects AI literacy research with self-efficacy theory, clarifying that many “literacy” measures function as assessments of perceived competence. Methodologically, it integrates PCA, counterfactual analysis, and Blinder–Oaxaca decomposition to disentangle the structure and origins of gendered AI self-efficacy, providing a rigorous model for interdisciplinary inquiry. Practically, by identifying the dimensions of self-reported AI literacy most affected by gender biases, it offers evidence to guide targeted policy interventions.

## 5. Limitation and future research directions

This study has several limitations. First, its cross-sectional design precludes causal inference; future longitudinal studies are needed to track how adolescents' AI literacy and self-efficacy evolve over time. Second, the data are confined to one national context, limiting cross-cultural generalizability. Comparative research across different cultural and institutional settings would shed light on whether the observed gender patterns are unique to China or more universal. Third, while our index was rigorously constructed, it remains based on self-reports. Self-reported AI literacy is treated here as a reflection of AI self-efficacy; however, the two constructs are conceptually distinct—this conceptual gap may limit interpretation. Future research should incorporate performance-based assess- ments of AI literacy alongside self-reported measures to provide a fuller picture of adolescents' competencies. Fourth, we acknowledge that our survey sample does not fully represent all Chinese adolescents; the specific sampling method could still be improved to enhance representativeness of the overall adolescent population in China. Finally, the Blinder–Oaxaca decomposition carries meth- odological limitations. The approach assumes linearity of the relationship between predictors and outcomes, additivity of effects, and correct model specification. These assumptions may be restrictive in the context of complex, multidimensional constructs like AI literacy. Our use of the decomposition is therefore intended as an illustrative tool to highlight the relative contributions of observable versus unexplained factors, rather than as a definitive causal estimate. Future work might explore alternative methods—such as nonlinear decomposition models, structural equation modeling, or machine learning approaches—to test the robustness of these findings.

Taken together, these limitations underscore the need for more diverse data sources, refined measurement strategies, and meth- odological pluralism. Future studies could build on this work by combining longitudinal and cross-cultural designs, integrating self- reported and performance-based measures, and further unpacking intersectional inequalities (e.g., urban–rural, socioeconomic sta- tus) to better inform inclusive AI education policies.
